title: sort() with no comparator
reveal:
9, not 10.

Array.prototype.sort with no comparator converts every element to a string and orders by UTF-16 code units, so [10, 9, 1] sorts as "1", "10", "9" and comes back as [1, 10, 9]. Numbers need a comparator:

    xs.sort((a, b) => a - b);   // ascending
    xs.sort((a, b) => b - a);   // descending

Two more details that bite:
  - sort() mutates the array in place AND returns that same array, so `const ys = xs.sort()` is a second name for xs, not a copy. toSorted() (ES2023) is the copying version.
  - undefined elements are moved to the end and never passed to your comparator, so a comparator cannot rescue them.

The algorithm itself has been required to be stable since ES2019 - equal elements keep their original order - which is what makes sorting by one key and then another a valid way to sort by both.
